newsitem.title: USA: US Justice urges FCC to reject Ameritech bid.
newsitem.headline: US Justice urges FCC to reject Ameritech bid.

text.p: The Justice Department urged federal phone regulators Wednesday to reject Ameritech Corp's bid to offer long-distance service in Michigan, saying the Baby Bell had yet to fully open its local phone monopoly to competition.

The department's recommendation to the Federal Communications Commission is a major blow to Chicago-based Ameritech's effort to enter the $80 billion long-distance business by offering service from its local-calling region.
And it represents the second time the department has advised the FCC to reject a Baby Bell long-distance request. The Bells have yet to win approval to get into long distance.

The department noted, however, that Ameritech has made "important progress" in opening its local phone network in Michigan -- but not enough to satisfy the requirements of last year's big communications law.
Under the law, a regional Bell can offer long-distance phoning from its own region once the FCC rules the carrier has met a 14-point checklist.
The list is designed to show a Bell has opened its local phone network to competitors -- such as long-distance companies or cable-television operators.

The law requires the agency to give "substantial weight" to the Justice Department's recommendation. Last month, the department urged the FCC to reject SBC Communications Inc's application to offer long-distance service in Oklahoma.

"As a result of Ameritech's efforts and cooperation with the department, as well as the state of Michigan's leadership in removing legal and economic barriers to entry, local competition is beginning to take root in Michgan," Acting Assitant Attorney General Joel Klein said in a statement.
But Klein added that Ameritech had not yet fully met the checklist and that the company has not yet demonstrated that its markets are fully and irreversibly open to competition.

In particular, the department said Ameritech had not met two checklist requirements: one allowing competitors to direct the routing of calls, and another relating to the local transport system for carrying local calls.
The department also detailed shortcomings relating to the leasing of Ameritech's local phone network.

Ameritech asked the FCC on May 21 for permission to offer long-distance service in Michigan, one of the five Midwestern states in which the company provides local calling. The FCC is scheduled to make a final decision by August 19.
Ameritech has 3.5 million customers in Michigan. The carrier values the long-distance market in its five-state territory at about $9 billion a year.
Earlier this year Ameritech was forced to withdraw its initial long-distance application because of numerous errors.
Meanwhile, the FCC is expected soon to rule on SBC's application to offer long-distance service, following the Justice Department's recommendation that it reject the bid.
Analysts expect the FCC to follow that advice.
